scalesUsed.notes: G - A - B - C - D - E - F# - G
scalesUsed.application: Harmonic foundation for the chord progression and vocal melody
The iconic intro riff and lead fills are built from this scale

keyAndScale.modalCharacter: Ionian (Major) with a bright, upbeat feel
keyAndScale.relativeMinor: E minor is the relative minor of G major

mainProgression.description: A timeless I-IV-I-V progression that drives the verse with bright, upbeat energy. This is one of the most common and memorable progressions in pop-rock music, with the vi chord adding depth in the chorus.

sectionProgressions.description: The main verse uses this four-chord cycle with two bars per chord, creating a rolling, feel-good momentum
The 'sha la la la la' chorus uses the same progression but with more energetic, sing-along delivery
The bridge introduces Em for a brief reflective moment before returning to the upbeat main progression

harmonicFunction: G (I) - Bright, stable tonic that establishes the cheerful character
C (IV) - Subdominant providing gentle harmonic motion away from home
D (V) - Dominant chord that creates the pull back to G, driving the progression forward
Em (vi) - Relative minor adding a brief wistful quality in the bridge

techniques.name: Open Chord Strumming
techniques.description: Bright, energetic strumming of open G, C, D, and Em chords with a driving eighth-note rhythm that carries the entire song

notes: G: 320003 (or 320033 with pinky) - standard open G major
C: X32010 - standard open C major
D: XX0232 - standard open D major
Em: 022000 - standard open E minor
Use a bright, consistent down-up strumming pattern
Emphasize downbeats to match the song's energetic feel
sequence: Strum G major for two bars
Transition to C major for two bars
Return to G major for two bars
Move to D major for two bars
Repeat the pattern for each verse and chorus
tips: Practice chord changes G-to-C and G-to-D separately before combining
Keep the strumming wrist relaxed at 150 BPM to avoid fatigue
Anchor the ring finger on the 3rd fret of the B string for G-to-C transitions
Strum all six strings on G and Em, avoid the lowest string on C and D
details.progression: G - C - G - D (verse) / Em - C - G - D (bridge)

techniques.name: Intro Riff (Optional)
techniques.description: The iconic guitar riff that opens the song, one of the most recognizable intros in rock history, based on the G major pentatonic scale

notes: Based on G major pentatonic scale on the D, G, and B strings around frets 0-4
Uses a bouncy, rhythmic pattern that mirrors the vocal melody
The riff follows the chord tones of G-C-G-D
Can be simplified by just playing the chord changes instead
Uses alternate picking for the quick single-note passages
sequence: Start on the G note sliding into position
Walk up through G major scale tones over the G chord
Transition to C chord tones for the IV chord section
Return to G chord tones before walking to D chord tones
End the riff pattern on the D chord leading back to G
tips: Learn the strumming version first before tackling the riff
The riff uses alternate picking for the quick passages
Keep the notes crisp and clean with good fretting hand pressure
Practice the riff slowly and gradually increase to 150 BPM
details.progression: G - C - G - D (single-note riff over chord changes)

techniques.name: Quick Chord Transitions at Speed
techniques.description: Rapidly switching between G, C, D, and Em chords at 150 BPM, building the speed and accuracy needed for uptempo rock strumming

notes: G to C: Middle and ring fingers shift from 5th and 6th strings to 5th and 4th strings
C to G: Reverse the above movement, adding pinky on 1st string
G to D: Lift off G shape and reform D shape on strings 1-3
D to Em: Simple transition - place two fingers onto 5th and 4th strings
The fast tempo demands efficient, minimal finger movement
sequence: Practice G to C transition 20 times slowly
Practice G to D transition 20 times slowly
Practice C to D transition 20 times slowly
Practice D to Em transition 20 times slowly
Chain them together: G-C-G-D then Em-C-G-D
tips: Keep fingers close to the fretboard during transitions
Use common anchor fingers where possible between shapes
Start at half tempo (75 BPM) and gradually increase speed
The faster tempo will come naturally with muscle memory
details.progression: G - C - G - D - Em - C - G - D

sections.name: Intro
sections.description: The famous opening riff that sets the upbeat tone - one of the most instantly recognizable guitar intros in rock history
notes: Iconic riff built on G major pentatonic
Establishes the bright, nostalgic mood
Beginners can substitute with strumming the chord progression
Riff repeats twice before the verse begins

sections.name: Verse
sections.description: Upbeat verse with steady strumming over the G-C-G-D progression supporting the nostalgic storytelling lyrics
notes: Two bars per chord at 150 BPM
Keep strumming bright and consistent
Leave space for the vocal melody to breathe
The verse progression repeats for each lyrical phrase

sections.name: Chorus (Sha La La)
sections.description: The iconic the signature singalong section - one of rock's greatest audience participation moments
notes: Same chord progression as the verse
Strumming gets slightly more energetic
the signature vocal melody is the hook everyone knows
Great section for audience participation at gigs

sections.name: Bridge
sections.description: A brief reflective bridge introducing the Em chord for emotional contrast before returning to the verse energy
notes: Em introduces a wistful, reflective quality
Provides dynamic contrast to the bright verses
Transitions back into the upbeat chorus
Only appears once in the song structure

sections.name: Outro
sections.description: Final chorus repetitions with the signature refrain building energy to the song's joyful conclusion
sections.progression: G - C - G - D (repeat to end)
notes: Repeated chorus progression building to finale
Full energy strumming with sing-along vocals
Maintain steady tempo through the final repetitions
Classic fade-out ending in the original recording

alternatives: Fender Stratocaster (for the recorded electric tone)
Any dreadnought acoustic for campfire version
Nylon string classical guitar works in a pinch
guitar.pickup: Acoustic preferred; if electric, use middle or bridge pickup for brightness

amp.recommended: Fender Twin Reverb or any clean-tone amp
alternatives: Any amp set to a clean channel

settings.bass: 4-5 (tight low end to keep strumming defined)

effects.reverb: Light spring reverb for classic 1960s vibe
effects.other: No capo needed. No effects required - plug in and play.

beginner.focus: Learn the four open chord shapes and basic strumming at a moderate tempo
steps: Learn open G, C, and D chord shapes individually until clean
Practice switching between G and C smoothly
Practice switching between G and D smoothly
Combine into the full G-C-G-D progression at slow tempo (75 BPM)

intermediate.focus: Play at full tempo with the Em bridge section and confident strumming
steps: Learn the Em chord and practice the bridge section (Em-C-G-D)
Gradually build speed toward 150 BPM with a metronome
Play through the full song structure without stopping
Learn the simplified version of the intro riff

advanced.focus: Master the full intro riff, add vocals, and perform the complete arrangement
steps: Learn the full intro riff at tempo with clean alternate picking
Add dynamics between verse and chorus sections
Practice singing while strumming the full song
Play along with the original Van Morrison recording

commonMistakes: Slowing down during chord transitions at the fast 150 BPM tempo
Strumming too hard - keep it bright and bouncy, not aggressive
Forgetting the Em in the bridge and playing G instead
Trying to learn the intro riff before mastering the chords - chords first
practiceRoutine: Warm up with G-C-D chord changes for 5 minutes
Practice the full verse progression (G-C-G-D) with a metronome at 120 BPM
Add the bridge section (Em-C-G-D) and practice transitions
Run through the full song structure without stopping
focusAreas: Fast and clean chord transitions at 150 BPM
Consistent strumming rhythm without slowing at chord changes
Song form awareness - knowing where each section starts
metronomeWork: Increase by 10 BPM increments until reaching 150 BPM
Practice strumming pattern alone on muted strings at full tempo
Play through full song at 150 BPM with metronome for timing accuracy
